Before we begin this evening's meeting, I'd also like to take a moment to recognize
the launch of Waterloo Region's We All Belong Here campaign, a powerful region-wide anti-hate
campaign designed to strengthen belonging and confront hate in all its forms. Belonging is one
of the most basic human needs. It is the foundation of a healthy, connected and thriving city. Yet we
know that many people in our community continue to experience discrimination, exclusion, and
identity-based harm. Kitchener is home to many new Canadians and ensuring that everyone feels
welcome and valued is vital to the strength and future of our city. As part of the community
safety and well-being plan and together with the Region of Waterloo and community partners,
the Combating Hate Action Table has developed the We All Belong Here Anti-Hate Campaign.
This region-wide initiative, represented by the artwork of Indigenous designer Katie Wilhelm,
aims to reduce hate and shape a city where everyone feels welcome, respected and celebrated
for who they are. This initiative reflects the values at the heart of the City of Kitchener's
strategic plan, which prioritizes building a caring, inclusive community. Over the past two years,
More than 30 partners, including municipalities, school boards and local organizations,
have come together to address, hate and co-create meaningful solutions.
Their dedication shows what is possible when a community chooses unity over division.
For me, the importance of belonging is deeply personal. Arriving in Canada as a young immigrant,
I experienced firsthand what it means to build a life in a new place together with my parents.
navigating unfamiliar systems, embracing new cultures, and finding connection in a community that welcomed us.
That sense of inclusion shaped my journey and my commitment to ensuring Kitchener remains a city where everyone feels they have a place to call home.
But creating a city where we all feel we belong isn't just the responsibility of organizations.
It is something we all share.
As residents and as leaders in Kitchener, we each have the power to shape the culture of our city.
We can help by taking the pledge to stand against hate, speak up and report it when you see it or experience hate,
and support those impacted and encourage others to do the same.
Together, we can build a city where everyone feels safe to be their authentic selves
and where every person is valued and celebrated for who they are.
This shared commitment reflects Council's ongoing vision of creating an inclusive city, one where belonging is not just an aspiration, but a lived experience for all.
Let us continue to lead with courage, with compassion, with kindness, and with commitment.
Because in Kitchener, we all belong here.
